title: Wall Street's top bosses shrug off rupee slide to double down on India
excerpt: Blackstone expects to double its India assets to $100 billion while Brookfield plans to deploy over $100 billion in five years — even as foreign investors pull $30 billion from Indian stocks.
body:
• The bet: Blackstone president Jon Gray told Bloomberg that outside the U.S., India is the world's most liquid market — the easiest place to get an IPO done this year — and the firm expects its India assets under management to double to $100 billion in the coming years.
  • The numbers behind the rush: Brookfield CEO Connor Teskey plans India investments exceeding $100 billion over five years, up from about $30 billion in 2025; Goldman Sachs has injected at least $500 million into its India banking franchise; India's Global Capability Centers passed 1,800 in 2025, are projected to exceed 2,400 by 2030, and generated around $100 billion in revenue last fiscal year.
  • The pain points they're looking past: Roughly $30 billion in foreign portfolio outflows from Indian stocks this year, a slumping rupee, rising inflation and high corporate taxes — with India ranking among the worst-performing equity markets of 2026 — plus SEBI enforcement actions against foreign trading desks.
  • What this means for readers watching India: The boom is powered by domestic money as much as Wall Street's — IPO banker fees in India now average 1.86% of deal value (above Hong Kong's ~1.5%). If you invest in Indian equities, note the split: record IPO liquidity and sticky domestic flows on one side, currency depreciation and $30 billion in foreign outflows on the other — hedge rupee exposure rather than buying the growth headline alone.

The bosses land in Delhi

In recent months, a string of Wall Street chiefs have landed in India to court businesses and the government. Citigroup's Jane Fraser met Prime Minister Narendra Modi; JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon met the finance minister. Both firms are working on the IPO of Mukesh Ambani's digital services giant Jio Platforms, expected later this year.

"For us, outside of the United States, India is the most liquid market — the easiest place to get an IPO done in the world this year."

— Jon Gray, president, Blackstone

Gray and other financial heavyweights acknowledge the challenges — rising inflation and the falling rupee. Yet Gray said Blackstone has had strong success in areas like its logistics portfolio, where underlying demand is powerful enough to compensate for currency depreciation.

Context & Background

Banks have been bolstering investment-banking and capital-markets teams — the average fee paid to bankers in India has risen to 1.86% of an IPO's value, per capital-markets data provider LSEG, above roughly 1.5% in Hong Kong — as Wall Street banks compete with each other, Japanese firms, and local houses like Kotak Mahindra Bank and Axis Bank in what has become one of the world's most competitive investment-banking markets.

Private equity, private credit and sovereign wealth funds are committing ever deeper pools of capital, while high-frequency trading firms like Citadel Securities and hedge funds like Millennium Management have built a presence — a turnaround from a few years ago, when PE investors had limited options to exit Indian investments, let alone at substantial profits.

Impact & Analysis

Underpinning it all is the rapid financialization of Indian household savings. Indians save $500 billion annually in financial assets, with almost 50% still in cash and deposits, per Macquarie analysts. "Rapid financialization of household savings is creating a durable pool of domestic capital to support private-sector investment," said Sonjoy Chatterjee, chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs India.

India's Global Capability Centers have evolved from 1990s back offices into mission-critical cogs of global finance: more than 1,800 in 2025, projected to exceed 2,400 by 2030 per Dun & Bradstreet, generating around $100 billion in revenue last fiscal year — JPMorgan alone employs about 60,000 people at its India centers. And GIFT City, Modi's low-tax hub in Gujarat, is drawing banks in fast: HSBC has built a $23 billion balance sheet there in under six years, and Citi's assets there are likely to reach $3 billion by end-2026 from about $350 million last December.

The pain points — and what's next

The risks are not abstract. India's markets have taken a hit this year as the oil-importing country's currency slumped and inflation rose with higher crude prices; foreign portfolio institutions have pulled about $30 billion from domestic stocks in pursuit of AI opportunities elsewhere. High corporate taxes and the rupee's decline leave foreign firms smaller dollar profits to repatriate.

Regulators are tightening as markets deepen. Indian retail traders lost more than $9 billion trading equity futures and options in the year ended March, pushing SEBI to clamp down on the derivatives boom — and it has taken enforcement action against a JPMorgan Mauritius unit and Jane Street over alleged manipulation, both contested.

Still, the bets keep coming — on the Jio IPO, on GCCs, on GIFT City, on the $4 trillion economy opening further to foreign money. Read the full story at Summa Money.
